ORIGINAL RESEARCH article

Front. Environ. Sci., 03 November 2026

Sec. Environmental Economics and Management

Volume 14 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2026.1963403

Network mechanisms and rule-of-law safeguards of comprehensive land consolidation in enhancing production-living-ecological space functions: evidence from township-level panel data in Zhejiang Province

  • WY

    Wujian Yang 1

  • JW

    Juan Wang 2

  • XM

    Xiting Mei 3*

  • 1. Library, Zhejiang A&F University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China

  • 2. School of Economics and Management, Zhejiang A&F University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China

  • 3. School of International Law, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Wuhan, Hubei, China

Article metrics

View details

Abstract

Introduction:

Whole-region comprehensive land consolidation (WRCLC), as a spatial governance approach integrating “all elements, all regions, the whole process, and the entire chain,” is of great significance for optimizing regional production–living–ecological space (PLES) functions.

Methods:

Existing studies have not yet systematically examined, from the holistic perspective of PLES functions, the spatial network mechanism and safeguard pathways of WRCLC at the macro level. Therefore, based on township-level panel data from Zhejiang Province for 2015–2022, this study comprehensively employs a multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) model, social network analysis (SNA), and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to systematically investigate the network mechanism and institutional safeguard pathways through which the WRCLC pilot policy enhances PLES functions.

Results:

The results show that the WRCLC pilot policy significantly improved the comprehensive PLES function (by 0.0023 units); this finding is significant at the 1% level and remains robust after a series of robustness checks. Meanwhile, network mechanism analysis reveals that the policy indirectly enhances PLES functions by improving the spatial correlation network. Configuration analysis further identifies three differentiated pathways: the “capital–industry” synergy type, the “human–capital”-driven type, and the multi-element synergy type, revealing the multiple concurrent conditions and factor combination logic underlying policy effectiveness.

Discussion:

Based on these findings, it is recommended that governments, when promoting WRCLC, should pay attention to regional spatial structure and factor endowment differences, strengthen rule-of-law safeguards, and implement differentiated governance strategies to achieve holistic optimization and coordinated development of PLES functions.

1 Introduction

Territorial space is the fundamental carrier of human production and living practices and ecological development. The degree of coordination among production, living, and ecological spatial functions (hereinafter referred to as the “PLES functions”) directly affects the quality and resilience of regional sustainable development. However, rapid urbanization and industrialization worldwide continue to reshape territorial space use patterns. Data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) show that between 2001 and 2023, global agricultural land area decreased by 78 million hectares1, while built-up land expansion far outpaced population growth; land degradation affects approximately 40% of the global terrestrial area2. Against this backdrop, land consolidation, as a core policy instrument for optimizing territorial spatial allocation and addressing urban–rural development imbalances, has been widely implemented and has continued to evolve across countries. Germany, with the Flurbereinigungsgesetz (Land Consolidation Act) as its core, has formed a comprehensive land consolidation legal system covering the adjustment of land rights, parcel consolidation, public facility construction, and rural development3. Japan, through laws such as the Land Improvement Act4, the Act on Improvement of Agricultural Promotion Areas5, and the Land Readjustment Act6, has constructed land use and consolidation systems from aspects including the improvement of agricultural infrastructure, the protection of agricultural land and agricultural land use planning, and the reallocation of urban and rural land, respectively. Turkey, Law No. 3083 on Land Reform regarding Rearrangement of Land in Irrigated Areas7; Law No. 5403 on Soil Preservation and Land Utilization8, integrates land consolidation, land reallocation, agricultural structural adjustment, cultivated land protection, and land use control. The evolution of the land consolidation legal systems in the above countries indicates that land consolidation has gradually evolved from early engineering-oriented parcel adjustment into a composite governance tool integrating spatial planning, tenure reorganization, ecological restoration, and community development.

Since the 18th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, China has attached great importance to the protection and development of territorial space and has continuously strengthened top-level design. The Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China further explicitly proposed that it is necessary to “coordinate the advancement of county-level territorial space governance and steadily carry out comprehensive land consolidation across the entire area,” so as to build a regional economic layout and a territorial space system characterized by complementary advantages and high-quality development. The Land Administration Law of the People’s Republic of China establishes the basic norms for land use control, territorial spatial planning, cultivated land protection, and land consolidation9. Article 42 of the Law stipulates that the state encourages land consolidation; county and township (town) people’s governments shall organize rural collective economic organizations to carry out comprehensive consolidation of fields, water, roads, forests, and villages in accordance with the overall land use plan, so as to improve the quality of cultivated land, increase the effective area of cultivated land, and improve agricultural production conditions and the ecological environment; at the same time, the Law also provides for the obligation of land reclamation. Regulations for the Implementation of the Land Administration Law of the People’s Republic of China further refine the relevant systems of territorial spatial planning implementation10, cultivated land protection, land use control, and land reclamation. On the basis of the basic systems of land management, territorial spatial planning, and ecological protection established by existing laws and regulations, the national level has further, through the Guidelines for the Implementation of Comprehensive Land Consolidation (Trial), made detailed provisions on the implementation units, consolidation areas, and implementation plans, and project arrangements of comprehensive land consolidation. Localities have also formed corresponding implementation norms in light of their own resource conditions and governance needs11. The above laws, administrative regulations, and policy implementation documents no longer position land consolidation merely as a technical activity related to land use efficiency or agricultural production, but instead place it within the interrelated legal governance objectives of land use control, cultivated land protection, territorial spatial planning, rural revitalization, and ecological restoration.

At the local level, Zhejiang Province was the first to explore and advance comprehensive land consolidation integrating production, living, and ecological functions. Through whole-area planning and design, it rationally allocates agricultural land, construction land, and ecological land, aiming to systematically resolve the “zero-sum dilemma” between development and protection (Yu et al., 2021). Zhejiang Province has enacted dedicated Land Consolidation Regulations of Zhejiang Province, which systematically provide for the concept, planning, implementation, supervision and management, and legal liability of land consolidation12. These Regulations define land consolidation as the consolidation, reclamation, and development of unused or unreasonably used land for the purpose of increasing the effective area of cultivated land and improving the quality of cultivated land, and require that land consolidation adhere to the priority of ecological and environmental protection and safeguard the rights of land right holders to information, participation, and supervision. In addition, Article 36 of the Territorial Spatial Planning Regulations of Zhejiang Province further provides that county (city, district) people’s governments shall, in accordance with the requirements of territorial spatial planning, formulate land comprehensive consolidation plans and, through the implementation of land consolidation, village improvement, and consolidation of inefficient urban land, systematically advance the comprehensive consolidation of fields, water, roads, forests, and villages, so as to promote the optimization of territorial spatial layout and the development of industrial agglomeration13. Thus, local regulations have incorporated comprehensive land consolidation into the institutional framework of territorial spatial planning implementation and economical and intensive land use. At the same time, laws and administrative regulations such as the Law of the People’s Republic of China on Urban and Rural Planning14, Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Promotion of Rural Revitalization15, and the Regulation on Land Reclamation16 provide supplementary normative bases for land consolidation from aspects including urban and rural spatial planning, rural ecological governance, and the restoration of damaged land. As a result, comprehensive land consolidation has formed a multi-level institutional arrangement ranging from laws and regulations to policy implementation rules and then to specific local practices. However, because the specific requirements of norms at different levels still differ in terms of planning articulation, departmental coordination, project implementation, and interest coordination, the implementation of comprehensive land consolidation still exhibits strong local institutional dependence. At present, comprehensive land consolidation has moved from the pilot stage to a stage of in-depth nationwide advancement, becoming a key platform for implementing territorial spatial planning and an important institutional vehicle for advancing the modernization of spatial governance. Therefore, establishing a scientific evaluation system and exploring the mechanisms and enhancement pathways through which pilot policies for comprehensive land consolidation affect the “PLES functions” have important policy reference value for promoting the sustainable development of territorial space.

Early studies mostly explored the theoretical logic of comprehensive land consolidation from a qualitative perspective, focusing on the interaction between land consolidation and spatial restructuring. Related studies have pointed out that comprehensive land consolidation promotes spatial restructuring through measures such as agricultural land consolidation, construction land consolidation, and ecological protection and restoration, exerting systemic effects on rural production, living, and ecological spaces (Gao et al., 2024). Some studies have used micro-survey data and case analysis to preliminarily reveal the impact of comprehensive land consolidation on production. Research shows that this policy significantly promotes land transfer and facilitates the transformation of agricultural organizational and operational modes, agricultural business scope, and agricultural production methods (Huanxin et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2026). However, other studies have found that comprehensive land consolidation still largely follows the traditional land consolidation approach of “emphasizing tasks, engineering, and indicators,” which cannot meet the goals of sustainable development and runs counter to the long-term objectives of rural revitalization (Jin et al., 2022). As an important indicator of regional sustainable development, the coordination of “production-living-ecological” spatial functions has irreplaceable value for systematically evaluating policy effects. In addition, some studies have noted that the integration relationship among “production-living-ecological” spaces is no longer limited to the traditional linear model but exhibits complex spatial network structural characteristics (Xiang et al., 2025). Therefore, there is an urgent need to systematically discuss the network mechanisms and enhancement pathways of comprehensive land consolidation at the macro level from the perspective of “production-living-ecological” spatial functions. Meanwhile, the relationships among “production-living-ecological” spatial functions are no longer confined to the traditional linear coupling model but present complex spatial network structural characteristics. Empirical studies at the metropolitan area scale (Yuan et al., 2024) show that the spatial correlation network of “production-living-ecological” functions has significant core–periphery structure and polycentric nested characteristics, and factor flows and functional spillover effects are transmitted among townships through transportation corridors, industrial chains, and ecological networks. This finding imposes new requirements on the policy design of comprehensive land consolidation, namely, consolidation activities should not only focus on optimizing factor allocation within a single township but also attend to cross-township spatial correlation effects and functional synergy mechanisms. However, existing studies remain unclear about how comprehensive land consolidation affects “production-living-ecological” spatial functions through spatial network mechanisms at the macro level (Xu et al., 2025). Moreover, at the institutional level, some studies have found that the implementation effectiveness of comprehensive land consolidation is highly dependent on local institutional arrangements and factor combinations. Different resource endowments, staffing arrangements, and governance conditions can lead to differentiated governance pathways and ultimately produce different policy effects (Zhang et al., 2026). Existing studies mostly focus on the independent influence of a single institutional factor on consolidation outcomes (Jing et al., 2024) or summarize typical models based on case experience (Tong et al., 2025), but rarely analyze, from a holistic perspective, the concurrent effects of the interactions among multiple institutional and resource factors on the improvement of “production-living-ecological” spatial functions. As a result, they struggle to explain the sources of differences in policy effects under different factor endowment conditions. Based on the gaps in existing research, this study takes townships in Zhejiang Province that were among the earliest to carry out comprehensive land consolidation pilots as the research object, uses township-level panel data from 2015 to 2022, systematically evaluates the net effect of the pilot policy on improving “production-living-ecological” spatial functions, further identifies the spatial network mechanisms through which the policy operates, and, through configurational analysis, summarizes and distills institutional safeguard pathways under different factor conditions, so as to provide empirical support and theoretical reference for optimizing the policy design of comprehensive land consolidation in China (see Figure 1).

2 Theoretical analysis

2.1 The direct impact of the WRCLC pilot policy on PLES functions

WRCLC uses townships as the basic implementation unit, taking into account diverse regional factors and the coordination and integration of departments and human-land relationships. It involves the consolidation of agricultural land, construction land, and rural ecological protection and restoration, making it a crucial platform for land spatial planning and a strong spatial support for rural revitalization (Zhou et al., 2024). At the broader spatial level, WRCLC is grounded in the theory of spatial production and governance modernization. Through scientific planning and systematic rectification, it promotes the reconstruction and optimization of national land space. It breaks the fragmented model of traditional land consolidation and realizes the coordinated arrangement and rational layout of agricultural, construction, and ecological land, thus enhancing the integrated benefits of the PLES functions. In the dimension of production space, the policy, based on resource allocation theory, not only directly enhances the quality of cultivated land and agricultural productivity through agricultural land consolidation, but also provides critical spatial support for the integration and upgrading of rural industries through the revitalization and reuse of construction land, thereby activating endogenous development momentum. In the transformation of living space, the policy profoundly reflects human-centered development and livability. By improving infrastructure and public services while emphasizing the protection of rural landscapes and cultural context during the consolidation process, it achieves an organic unity of modern living convenience and the unique charm of rural areas. Finally, in the ecological dimension, the policy implements landscape ecology and sustainable development theories. Through systematic protection and restoration projects and the construction of ecological networks, it enhances the stability and service functions of ecosystems, ensuring ecological security and biodiversity. In conclusion, WRCLC is guided by a systematic theoretical framework, achieving the comprehensive governance goal of synergizing the PLES functions Accordingly, this study derives its first hypothesis:

H1: The WRCLC pilot policy positively influences the functions of the PLES.

2.2 The network mechanism of the WRCLC pilot policy on PLES functions

Based on SNA theory (Li et al., 2025) and the practice of WRCLC, this policy can reshape the structural relationships among the PLES functions within a region, thereby promoting their functional enhancement. Specifically, core indicators such as degree centrality, closeness centrality, and betweenness centrality can be employed for explanation, corresponding respectively to the network centrality, connectivity, and “bridge” roles of pilot townships PLES functions within the entire region (Su et al., 2025).

Firstly, in terms of degree centrality, the WRCLC policy does not target the fragmented improvement of individual plots or functions. Instead, it undertakes integrated planning and holistic optimization of PLES. According to the “Multi-Plan Integration (MPI)” theory (Zhao and Li, 2023), this approach can break the original fragmented and isolated spatial utilization patterns, promoting a transition of township land use functions from singular to synergistic. Such functional strengthening and optimization enhance the output capacity and attractiveness of pilot townships in the regional PLES functions network, whether as suppliers of production factors, providers of ecological services, or carriers of livable spaces. Consequently, the “connection channels” for element flows, functional complementarities, and spatial linkages with other townships are significantly increased. This is reflected in a growth in the number of direct connections within the network, namely, an effective increase in degree centrality, thereby moving the township from the periphery to the center of the network and establishing it as a key node for the circulation of PLES functions.

Secondly, in terms of closeness centrality, one of the core tasks of WRCLC is to construct an efficient and coordinated land space structure, which directly influences the cost and efficiency of spatial connections. Through the implementation of land ownership adjustments, integration of transportation infrastructure, and the construction of ecological networks, this policy can significantly reduce spatial barriers both within and outside rural towns. According to the theory of spatial accessibility (Lloyd, 2023), the elimination of spatial barriers means that the physical distance and cost distance for functional transmission from the pilot rural town to any other node in the network are shortened. Meanwhile, the shorter the path, the more direct the connection. As a result, the pilot rural town’s dependence on intermediate nodes for accessing resources, radiating functions, and exerting influence becomes lower, enhancing its capacity for independent action and rapid response. Therefore, WRCLC improves spatial connectivity efficiency, bringing the pilot rural town closer to a core position of “accessibility in all directions”, thereby increasing its closeness centrality.

Thirdly, in terms of betweenness centrality, WRCLC can significantly enhance the intermediary centrality of the pilot area’s PLES functions by shaping regional functional hubs, thereby strengthening its strategic position in controlling the flow of resource information. The macro effect of comprehensive consolidation lies in reshaping the spatial functional structure of the region, which often leads to the pilot rural town undertaking specific functional roles, such as agricultural industrial zones, ecological service zones, etc. When pilot townships leverage core functions that have been strengthened or newly introduced through governance interventions to connect different parts or functional modules within the network, previously low-efficiency nodes may experience intensified interactions due to their “bridging” role. This allows the pilot rural town to gain powerful connectivity in the PLES functional network, enabling it to influence or even control the flow paths and efficiency of resources, information, and energy between other towns, effectively increasing its intermediary centrality. Accordingly, this study derives its second hypothesis:

H2: WRCLC helps promote the enhancement of the spatial correlation network of PLES functions.

2.3 The configuration framework of the WRCLC pilot policy and PLES functions

Grounded in the theory of the regional man-land relationship system (Jin et al., 2020), the interaction between humans and land is evidently multi-element and complex, involving the interconnection of factors such as population, land, and economy. A systematic analysis approach is required to represent the underlying mechanisms of this relationship. The configurational perspective, with its focus on the phenomena of “multiple conjunctural causation” and “equifinality”, can effectively explain the non-linear relationships and causal asymmetries in complex systems. This perspective is particularly useful in exploring the multi-element combinatory paths through which comprehensive land consolidation impacts the spatial functions of the PLES. In this context, this paper adopts the configurational perspective to categorize the various factors in the human-environment system into core and peripheral systems, and develops a theoretical framework to analyze the synergy between the “human–land–industry” and “finance–governance–rights” dimensions. This framework systematically explains the diverse pathways through which comprehensive land consolidation promotes the enhancement of the PLES functions (Luo et al., 2024).

The core system, comprising the three fundamental elements of “human–land–industry” (Xu and Zhang, 2023; Sun and Lu, 2023; He, 2018), interacts synergistically to constitute the endogenous driving force behind the evolution of regional spatial functions. Among them, “human” are the principal actors and key decision-makers of spatial demand, as the pursuit of livability drives settlement restructuring. Additionally, rational economic agents, as represented by new types of agricultural business entities and rural entrepreneurs, can proactively identify policy opportunities and lead the rectification practices. By optimizing land use decisions, they directly affect the efficiency of production spaces and the configuration of ecological spaces. The “land” element is the material carrier of spatial functions and the core object of rectification efforts. By implementing projects like farmland rectification, construction land reorganization, and ecological restoration, it directly reshapes the physical form, utilization structure, and functional relationships of the PLES. The “industry” element serves as the economic engine that stimulates spatial vitality. Rectification efforts guide the optimization of industrial spatial layouts, promote agricultural scale management, and rural industrial integration (RII). This injects continuous momentum into production spaces and supports the sustainability of improved living quality and ecological protection through industrial linkages.

The peripheral system provides critical external support for the operation of the core system, encompassing three key elements: “finance,” “governance,” and “rights.” The “finance” element is the material foundation for advancing the governance process. By relying on financial tools such as special government funds, private capital introduction, and ecological compensation, a diversified funding pool is created to ensure the enhancement of the PLES functions. The “governance” element serves as the organizational hub for coordinated progress. Efficient governance conditions can effectively implement WRCLC policy across the region, promote the participation of multiple stakeholders in project development, and establish a strong endogenous driving mechanism. This creates a stable and favorable external environment and internal driving force for the advancement of policy. The “rights” element is the institutional core for stimulating internal motivation. By clarifying the market-based transaction system and ensuring the rights and interests of farmers as key stakeholders in land consolidation, their enthusiasm and creativity for participating in the governance process are stimulated, thus providing institutional guarantees for the enhancement of the PLES functions.

From a configurational perspective, the core system and the peripheral system do not exist in isolation but are intertwined and synergize to collectively constitute a complex system through which WRCLC enhances PLES functions. On the one hand, the “human-land-industry” elements of the core system interact with and feedback on each other, forming the endogenous driving force for the evolution of regional spatial functions, providing target direction and practical foundation for the operation of the peripheral system. On the other hand, the “finance-governance-rights” elements of the peripheral system provide material support, organizational guarantees, and institutional incentives, creating favorable conditions for the operation of the core system and promoting its development to a higher level. This synergistic interaction between the core and peripheral systems enables WRCLC to apply multiple elements and means, achieving the systematic enhancement and optimization of the PLES functions. Accordingly, this study derives its third hypothesis:

H3: WRCLC promotes the enhancement of PLES functions through the synergistic coordination of “human-land-industry” and “finance-governance-rights” elements.

3 Materials and methods

3.1 Overview of the study area

Zhejiang Province is located in the southern wing of the Yangtze River Delta on the southeast coast of China, spanning 27°02′–31°11′N and 118°01′–123°10′E. It has a monsoon-influenced humid climate with concurrent rainfall and heat. The province has a land area of 105,500 km2, of which mountains account for 74.6%, water surfaces 5.1%, and flat land 20.3%. It is known as a region of “seven parts mountains, one part water, and two parts farmland,” and the contradiction between economic development and scarce land resources is prominent. Since 2018, Zhejiang Province has taken the lead in carrying out comprehensive land consolidation pilots, announcing three batches of township-level pilots in 2019, 2020, and 2021, respectively. Among them, the first and second batches of provincial-level pilots for comprehensive land consolidation and ecological restoration, announced on 6 June 2019 and 11 September 2020, totaled 497, while the 42 national-level pilots announced by the Ministry of Natural Resources in 2021 brought the total to 539. After excluding street-level pilots, samples with severe missing data, and samples affected by administrative division adjustments, only 4,312 valid observations were ultimately obtained (see Figure 2).

FIGURE 2

3.2 Data source

WRCLC pilot township data for Zhejiang Province came from the official websites of the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Natural Resources and the Ministry of Natural Resources of China (https://zrzyt.zj.gov.cn). Township-level indicators (administrative area, number of industrial enterprises, number of village committees) were taken from the China County Economic Statistical Yearbook (Township Volume) 2016–2023. Temperature data were obtained from Peng Shouzhang (2020) via the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/home). County-level control variables came from the Zhejiang Statistical Yearbook (2016–2023), with missing values filled by linear interpolation. Data on new agricultural business entities was sourced from the Tianyancha platform, filtering for region, industry, registration status, and establishment date to count registered and operating agriculture-related enterprises in pilot townships before and after the policy. Township land consolidation areas were retrieved from the “Supplementary Cultivated Land Projects and Parcel Information” portal of China’s Ministry of Natural Resources. Lists of Zhejiang’s specialty agricultural towns and agricultural machinery replacement demonstration towns were provided by the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Land transfer data came from the Zhejiang Online Land Use Rights Trading System. Nighttime light data originated from NOAA’s SNPP-VIIRS satellite data (https://ngdc.noaa.gov). Annual NPP and EVI data were derived from NASA’s MOD17A3HGF and MOD13A2 products, respectively. Landscape diversity data were extracted from Landsat imagery. Data on village collective economic income were obtained from the Department of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of Zhejiang Province.

3.3 Research methods

3.3.1 Baseline regression model

To account for the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of WRCLC implementation in Zhejiang Province, we adopt a multi-period DID model (Lu et al., 2025a). This method enables us to isolate the policy’s net impacts on PLES functions. The baseline model is defined below:

3.3.3 Spatial durbin model

To examine the spatial spillover effects of the pilot policy for comprehensive land consolidation on “production-living-ecological” spatial functions, this paper constructs a spatial difference-in-differences model. Following the research of LeSage and Pace (Lesage and Pace, 2009), the spatial Durbin model (SDM) is selected as the baseline model. The SDM simultaneously incorporates the spatial lag terms of both the dependent variable and the core explanatory variables, thereby effectively capturing the spatial transmission effects of the policy. In Equation 6, is the spatial weight matrix. In this paper, an inverse distance weight matrix is constructed using the reciprocal of the squared point distance between townships, i.e., . is the spatial autoregressive coefficient, which measures the influence of the “production-living-ecological” spatial functions of neighboring townships on those of the focal township. is the coefficient of the direct policy effect. is the coefficient of the spatial interaction term, reflecting the influence of the policy on the “production-living-ecological” spatial functions of neighboring townships. The meanings of the remaining variables are the same as above.

3.3.4 Mediation model

To mitigate power loss associated with multiple testing in the three-step approach, this study follows the two-step procedure developed by Jiang Ting (Jiang, 2022). in combination with the baseline regression model to explore mediation effects. First, the relationship between WRCLC pilot policy and PLES functions is examined using Equation 1. Subsequently, Equations 7–9 construct regression models between the pilot policy and mechanism variables to evaluate their impact on degree centrality, closeness centrality, and betweenness centrality. Finally, theoretical analysis determines the relationship between the pilot policy and the mechanism variables, with the specific models presented as follows:

Equations 7–9 are as follows: where represents the degree centrality, represents the closeness centrality, and represents the betweenness centrality. , , are constant terms; , , are the regression coefficients of the WRCLC pilot policy effects; represents the control variables, with , , as their coefficients, , , capture the individual fixed effects, , , represents the idiosyncratic error terms.

3.3.5 FsQCA approach

WRCLC is a complex system project, and its impact on the PLES functions is not achieved through a single policy or measure in isolation. Instead, it arises from the interplay and coordinated effects of various consolidation factors across different settings. Traditional econometric methods have the advantage of identifying the “net effect” of individual factors but struggle to reveal the concurrency of multiple factors, the substitution and complementarity between elements, as well as intricate causal mechanisms such as “equifinality”. To address these theoretical challenges, this study employs fsQCA for in-depth analysis (Wu et al., 2026).

FsQCA is a case-oriented analytical technique well-suited for handling complex causal relationships in small to medium-sized samples. It allows each region implementing comprehensive land consolidation to be viewed as a complex case, where systematic comparison can detect distinct arrangements of intervention elements that lead to high or non-high levels of PLES functions, thereby revealing the causal pathways. In this context, this paper further selects pilot samples to explore the configuration logic behind the policy’s effectiveness, aiming to clarify the pathways through which the “core-periphery” system enhances PLES functions.

3.4 Variable selection

3.4.1 Dependent variable

This study takes PLES functions—namely production, living, and ecological functions—as the dependent variable. Following the multi-functional rural evaluation framework proposed by Xu Kai et al. (Xu et al., 2023), the production space was assessed based on both the quantity and quality of cropland; the living space was evaluated using population density and nighttime illumination data; and the ecological space was measured through ecosystem service and landscape diversity index (LDI) (see Table 1).

Given that the various functions of PLES are quantified using different units, this study employed the range standardization normalization technique (Liu et al., 2026). Following the normalization of each indicator, the values were aggregated to formulate a composite index representing PLES functions, which was computed as follows:

In Equation 10, represents the township functional score of township unit , with a larger value indicating a stronger function; is the standardized value of indicator for township unit ; is the number of indicators; and is the weight of indicator .

3.4.2 Core independent variable

The WRCLC pilot policy constitutes the main independent variable of this analysis. Following related studies (Lu et al., 2025b), the implementation of the policy in a specific township during a given year is used as the criterion. If the policy was implemented in that year, this binary variable takes a value of 1 for pilot townships and 0 in all other cases.

3.4.3 Control variables

The control variables span both administrative levels. Township-level controls include administrative area, number of industrial enterprises, and temperature; county-level controls comprise economic development, industrial structure, government intervention, educational development, agricultural development, and technological innovation.

3.4.4 Mediating variable

Degree centrality, closeness centrality, betweenness centrality are employed as measures. Based on the SNA framework in spatial economics, the relational paths among nodes are quantified and node roles are identified. Specifically, degree centrality reflects the extent to which an individual township occupies a central position within the overall relational network; closeness centrality measures how freely a township operates without being restricted by other townships in the network.; and betweenness centrality measures the degree to which a township controls the relational.

3.4.5 Conditional variable

The “human” element is represented, following Liu Yang et al. (Liu et al., 2025), by the annual average number of newly established agricultural, forestry, animal husbandry, and fishery enterprises during the policy implementation period as a proxy variable. The “land” element is considered in terms of the spatial context, while the “industry” element includes four specific categories: Zhejiang’s Taobao towns, provincial characteristic agricultural strong towns, tourism-oriented towns, agricultural machinery replacement demonstration towns, plus one further category. The “finance” element is measured by the village collective economic income of each pilot township. The “governance” element, drawing on the study by Yao Linxiang and Lu Guangxi (Yao and Lu, 2023), is measured by the number of village committees per one million residents in each pilot township. Finally, the “rights” dimension is measured as the share of township land transferred via bidding, auction, and listing in total land transfer area, reflecting the level of land marketization at the township level (see Table 2).

These results demonstrate that the rehabilitation policy consistently enhances PLES functions, even after accounting for a broad set of township and county attributes.

4.2 Robustness test

4.2.1 Parallel trend test

Figure 3 displays the parallel trends test results, showing coefficient estimates and their confidence intervals for each period surrounding the policy implementation, derived from a dynamic model. In the pre-policy period (with 2018 as the baseline), all coefficients hover near zero, and their confidence bands contain zero, implying no statistically significant difference in pre-existing trends between the two groups. Following the policy, the coefficient turns significantly positive, indicating a sustained beneficial effect. Thus, the parallel trends assumption is met, and the test is passed.

FIGURE 3

4.2.2 The placebo test

To verify the robustness of the study’s conclusions and to control, as far as possible, for potential interference from unobserved factors on the estimated policy effects, this paper conducts a placebo test as a robustness check of the core findings (see Figure 4). By randomizing the treatment variable, 500 sampling simulations were performed, each employing the exact same model specification as in the baseline regression, and the respective regression coefficients and accompanying p-values were recorded. The simulated coefficients are centered near zero, with the overwhelming majority of p-values falling above the 0.1 threshold. The actual baseline estimate (0.0023) appears within the rightmost part of the simulated distribution, markedly outside its central range. This distribution implies that the significant baseline effect probably does not stem from random variation or model misspecification. Therefore, the treatment variable exerts a statistically meaningful influence on the outcome, and this influence is not an artifact of chance or incorrect model specification.

FIGURE 4

4.2.3 Additional robustness checks

Ensuring the robustness of the empirical findings, this study undertakes multiple sensitivity analyses, such as winsorization, the Propensity Score Matching Difference-In-Differences (PSM-DID) approach, exclusion of national-level pilot programs, and interactive fixed effects (See Table 4.). In column (1), all variables except the dependent variable and the core dependent variable are winsorized at the 1% level on each side; the main conclusions remain unchanged. Column (2) applies a 1:4 nearest-neighbor matching PSM-DID procedure with a caliper of 0.05 to mitigate sample selection bias, and the estimated policy effect remains statistically significant. Column (3) excludes national-level pilot policies to address potential systematic differences in policy implementation intensity, and the results remain robust. Column (4) further incorporates city-by-year interactive fixed effects to capture heterogeneous policy environments and development dynamics across prefecture-level cities over time; the core variable’s coefficient remains statistically significant.

5 Spatial correlation network of PLES functions

5.1 Spatial spillover effects

To investigate the spatial spillover effects of the pilot policy for comprehensive land consolidation on “production–living–ecological” spatial functions, the spatial Durbin model was introduced for analysis. The results are presented in Table 6. Although the spatial Durbin model can identify the spatial dependence structure of variables, its coefficients alone cannot directly reveal the specific magnitude of the variables’ effects. Therefore, the partial differentiation method was further employed to decompose the spatial effects of the pilot policy for comprehensive land consolidation (Meng et al., 2026), yielding its direct, indirect, and total effects, so as to more clearly understand its spatial pathways of influence on “production–living–ecological” spatial functions.

The effect decomposition results show that the direct, indirect, and total effects of the pilot policy for comprehensive land consolidation are all positive and pass the significance tests at the 1%, 10%, and 5% levels, respectively, indicating that the implementation of the local policy can not only optimize local “production–living–ecological” spatial functions but also generate positive demonstration and driving effects on neighboring areas through spatial correlation. This suggests that the optimization of “production–living–ecological” spaces does not occur in isolation but forms spatial linkages through cross-regional factor flows and coordinated development. The effect decomposition results for the control variables show that the total effects of industrial structure upgrading and economic development level are significantly positive, contributing to the synergistic improvement of spatial functions; the total effects of educational development level and the number of industrial enterprises are significantly negative, reflecting that uneven resource allocation and high-density industrial agglomeration constrain the optimization of “production–living–ecological” spaces.

5.2 Mechanism test

To further investigate the mechanisms through which the pilot policy for comprehensive land consolidation affects “production–living–ecological” (PLES) spatial functions, this paper takes township units in Zhejiang Province as the basis, constructs a PLES spatial function correlation network, and employs social network analysis to calculate topological indicators for each node, including degree centrality, closeness centrality, and betweenness centrality. On this basis, these network indicators are further incorporated into a causal mediation analysis framework to systematically test the mediating pathways through which the policy influences PLES functions by affecting townships’ positions in the spatial network. Table 7 reports the results of the mediation effect tests. Column (1) shows that the estimated coefficient of the policy on degree centrality is significantly positive at the 1% level, indicating that comprehensive land consolidation significantly enhanced the centrality of pilot townships in the PLES spatial correlation network, enabling them to establish direct connections with more nodes and thereby expanding their resource integration scope and influence within the local network. Specifically, through agricultural land consolidation, revitalization of construction land, ecological restoration, and industrial platform construction, pilot townships strengthened direct linkages with surrounding townships in terms of land quotas, capital, labor, and ecological products, forming local agglomeration effects. In Column (2), the coefficient of the policy on closeness centrality is also positively significant at the 1% level, indicating that land consolidation, through “multi-plan integration,” infrastructure connectivity, and ecological corridor construction, shortened the distance of factor flows among townships and improved the global accessibility of pilot townships in the regional network, making them less constrained by other nodes and enabling them to interact more efficiently with nodes across the entire network. It also promoted cross-township matching of ecological service supply and demand, thereby strengthening their role as central actors. In Column (3), the effect of the policy on betweenness centrality did not pass the significance test, reflecting that the policy did not significantly enhance the ability of pilot townships to serve as “structural bridges”; that is, their hub function in controlling connections among other nodes and guiding cross-regional resource flows has not yet been fully activated. Possible reasons are as follows: First, comprehensive land consolidation takes townships as the basic implementation unit, and administrative boundaries and assessment units remain relatively strong, so cross-township resource allocation and joint consolidation projects are relatively limited. Second, the policy implementation period is relatively short, and the formation of intermediary nodes and bridging functions requires longer-term network evolution and project accumulation. Third, multiple alternative paths exist in the PLES network, and a few non-pilot central towns may assume intermediary functions, resulting in insignificant changes in the betweenness centrality of pilot townships. Fourth, PLES improvement relies more on factor flows brought by direct connections and accessibility than on “control” over network paths. Combined with the effect decomposition of the spatial Durbin model, the direct, indirect, and total effects of the policy are all significantly positive, indicating that the policy improves PLES mainly through local direct improvement and neighborhood spillovers rather than through transmission via intermediary nodes. Taken together, the above results indicate that the pilot policy for comprehensive land consolidation optimizes “production–living–ecological” spatial functions mainly by enhancing the degree centrality and closeness centrality of townships.

5.3 Network structure of PLES functions in pilot areas

To further explore the network-based impact of WRCLC on regional PLES functions, this study selects Ningbo City and Jiaxing City in Zhejiang Province—both characterized by distinctive implementation features—as typical cases for comparative analysis (see Figure 5). Both cities have been included in the first batch of typical WRCLC pilot cases issued by the Ministry of Natural Resources, yet they differ in their implementation approaches and priorities. Ningbo emphasizes a holistic strategy of “resource reorganization, functional reshaping, spatial restructuring, industrial reconfiguration, and environmental regeneration.” Jiaxing, by contrast, focuses on “transforming fragmented farmland into consolidated fields” and has established the largest contiguous area of highest-quality cultivated land with the highest grade in the province. By constructing the spatial correlation network of PLES functions of townships in the two cities and calculating their centrality indicators. This study uncovers how the policy shapes the evolutionary features of the spatial network structure.

FIGURE 5

5.3.1 Analysis of network structure evolution in Ningbo City

In 2015, ahead of the pilot policy’s implementation, the PLES network in Ningbo City exhibited a typical “single-core–periphery” structure. Network centrality was highly concentrated in townships of the northern Hangzhou Bay area, including Yuyao, Cixi, Zhenhai, and Beilun, where centrality values reached the range of 18.001–21.000, forming a strong agglomeration and radiation pole of economic activity. In stark contrast, most townships in the southern counties of Ninghai and Xiangshan remained on the network periphery, with centrality values mostly below 13.000 and weak connections. At this stage, high-value areas of PLES functions were strictly confined to the northern core, indicating a tight coupling between network structure and the stage of economic growth. A significant development gradient and functional fragmentation existed between land and sea, and between the north and the south. By 2020, during the rollout of the pilot policy, driven by Ningbo’s WRCLC pilot program characterised by “systemic reconfiguration”, the network structure began to shift toward multi-polarisation and maritime integration. The absolute dominance of the northern core persisted, but its radiation range and connection intensity started to expand in multiple directions. A key change was the notable increase in the centrality of coastal townships with good port resources, such as Hepu and Shipu in Xiangshan County, which rose to a higher hierarchical level, signalling that the value of maritime space had been activated through consolidation. The network structure began to evolve from a single “inland economic monopole” toward a preliminary “land-sea coordination” configuration, with medium-to-high-value areas of spatial functionality showing a scattered diffusion trend along transport corridors and the coastline. By 2022, in the post-policy implementation period, Ningbo’s spatial network had evolved into a mature pattern characterised by “one core leading and three zones interacting”. The northern urban-economic core continued to play a leading role, but the drivers of the network became more diversified. The eastern coastal area, leveraging the integration of port resources and upgrading of port-side industries, developed a distinct maritime economic zone. The southern area, through ecological restoration and protection combined with the development of green industries, upgraded from an ecological “base” to a transformational “hub”. The western Siming Mountain area, serving as a critical ecological barrier, saw its structural function further clarified within the network. Corresponding to this multi-polar network, high-value areas of PLES functions exhibited a “scattered but well-distributed” pattern. This indicates that WRCLC, through systematic functional reshaping and spatial reorganisation, effectively broke the original path dependence, promoted a profound transition from a single “economically monopole-driven” to a “land–sea multi-element symbiosis”, and enhanced the overall resilience and collaborative efficiency of regional development.

5.3.2 Analysis of network structure evolution in Jiaxing City

In 2015, before the WRCLC pilot policy was rolled out, the PLES network in Jiaxing City exhibited a pronounced pattern of “single-pole concentration, stronger north and weaker south”. Network centrality was highly concentrated in townships located in northern Jiashan County and northeastern Pinghu City, adjacent to the border with Shanghai. Leveraging their geographical and industrial advantages, these areas developed strong regional radiation and factor agglomeration capacities. In contrast, townships in Haiyan County, southern Haining City, and western Tongxiang City remained at the network’s periphery, with generally low centrality and weak spatial connectivity. At this stage, high-value areas of PLES functions closely overlapped with the network core, indicating that the level of economic development was the dominant factor determining network position, and the overall network structure was unbalanced. By 2020, during the pilot implementation phase of the policy, with the advancement of consolidation projects such as “consolidating fragmented plots” and improving farmland quality and contiguity, the network structure began to undergo systemic reconfiguration. A notable change was the significant increase in centrality among townships in Tongxiang City and Haining City with strong agricultural endowments, which gradually evolved into emerging secondary cores. This shift directly resulted from the optimization of agricultural production space through land consolidation: large-scale, well-equipped farmland enhanced the nodal roles of these townships in regional agricultural supply and rural landscape systems. The network pattern transitioned from a “single-core” to a “dual-core” configuration, and high-value areas of spatial functionality correspondingly spread from north to south, demonstrating the initial effectiveness of policy intervention in reshaping the network structure. By 2022, in the post-policy implementation period, Jiaxing’s network pattern had evolved into a balanced development configuration characterized by “multi-core synergy and corridor connectivity”. The area centered on the “Tianfu Ten-Thousand-Mu Contiguous Farmland” zone emerged as a key growth pole in the network, with its centrality rising to among the highest in the city, standing alongside the original industrial core. Network connections became highly dense and balanced, and the earlier north–south gradient disparity largely disappeared. High- and medium-high-value areas of PLES functions became extensively contiguous, forming functional improvement corridors that spanned the municipal territory. This evolutionary trajectory clearly demonstrates that WRCLC—focused on arable land integration and quality enhancement—can systematically cultivate new network hubs by optimizing the production space carrier, effectively promoting the transformation of regional spatial networks from “single-pole dependence” to “multi-pole synergy”, and achieving coordinated improvements in PLES functions across the region.

6 Configuration path analysis

6.1 Data calibration

This study used fsQCA to investigate the intricate causal links that are both necessary and sufficient underlying the improvement of PLES functions, focusing on the interaction between “human–land–industry” factor configurations and “finance–governance–rights” mechanism configurations. A direct calibration strategy was adopted. The calibration thresholds for full membership, the transition point, and full non-membership were defined by the 95th percentile, median, and 5th percentile of each variable’s descriptive statistics, respectively. To resolve indeterminacy for cases exactly at 0.50, a constant of 0.001 was added to the membership value (Wagemann et al., 2016). Table 8 presents the calibration results in detail.

6.2 Necessity analysis

Necessity analysis serves as a foundational step in configurational research, as it identifies single necessary conditions for an outcome, that is, conditions that must be present for the outcome to occur. This study tests the necessity of each individual condition among the “core-periphery” factors. A consistency threshold of 0.9 is set as the evaluation criterion. According to Table 9, the consistency values for all condition variables are below this cutoff, implying that no single necessary condition alone can account for the enhancement of PLES functions in the study sample. This finding methodologically confirms that the effect of WRCLC on PLES follows a complex causal logic marked by multiple concurrencies. No individual factor serves as both necessary and sufficient for achieving success. Therefore, this result strongly justifies the need and rationale for conducting subsequent configurational analysis to identify multiple equivalent pathways.

6.3 Sufficiency analysis

The analysis is conducted using fsQCA 3.0 software to systematically investigate the factor configurations—encompassing human, land, industry, finance, governance, and rights—that drive high and non-high levels of PLES functions. For the configurational analysis, we adopt the following parameters: a case frequency cutoff of 1, a raw consistency level of 0.8 and a PRI consistency level of 0.65 These settings are designed to yield configurations that are both theoretically relevant and practically actionable. Second, considering that the mechanisms through which each antecedent condition affects PLES functions are context-dependent and that regional development characteristics differ significantly, this study follows a cautious principle in counterfactual analysis by not presupposing a fixed direction of influence for any antecedent condition. Consequently, three types of solutions are generated: complex, intermediate, and parsimonious. The intermediate solution is selected as the primary basis for interpretation. To differentiate the attributes of conditions, we investigate the subset relationship between the intermediate and parsimonious solutions. Specifically, a condition that appears in both solutions is designated as a core condition, while a condition appearing solely in the intermediate solution is treated as a peripheral condition. Table 10 reports the detailed configuration results for achieving high and non-high levels of PLES functions.

■ = presence of a core condition; ▲ = presence of a peripheral condition; □ = absence of a core condition; △ = absence of a peripheral condition; blank = condition may be present or absent.

6.3.1 Configurational path analysis of high production–living–ecological space functions

Configuration S1 is the “capital–industry” synergy type. Configuration S1a has “industry” and “finance” as core presence conditions, while “land” and “governance” are core absence conditions. This pathway covers 46.67% of the cases, with a consistency of 0.9122, indicating that even when the land and governance systems are not yet well developed, sufficient capital investment can still effectively promote the improvement of “production–living–ecological” (PLES) spatial functions. A typical case of this pathway is Xucun Town, Haining City. As a traditional home textile industry town, Xucun Town, building on the substantial capital accumulated in the home textile industry, vigorously promoted comprehensive land consolidation. Through sustained capital investment, it focused on implementing projects such as industrial park renovation, rural residential environment improvement, and river ecological restoration. Although there were deficiencies in cross-regional collaborative governance and the integration mechanism of rights and responsibilities, through concentrated capital investment and project-based advancement, it still significantly improved the region’s spatial functions, forming a typical model of “industrial capital-driven, project-based advancement.”Configuration S1b additionally has “people” as a core presence condition. This pathway covers 44.7% of the cases, indicating that human resource enhancement plays a key role in promoting PLES functions. The underlying logic is that cultivating new agricultural operating entities can stimulate endogenous development momentum in the region. A typical case of this pathway is Xincheng Town, Xiuzhou District, Jiaxing City. Xincheng Town established a cultivation and service system covering talent at different levels, while continuously advancing comprehensive land consolidation and urban quality improvement projects. Driven synergistically by talent and capital, the annual multiple cropping area of grain exceeded 100,000 mu, and it actively explored an “agriculture + cultural tourism” integration model, effectively promoting agricultural efficiency and spatial function improvement. Configuration S1c additionally has “rights” as a core presence condition. This pathway covers 44.58% of the cases, further indicating that a strong rights and responsibilities mechanism can effectively integrate capital and industrial resources. A typical case of this pathway is Puyuan Town, Tongxiang City. Building on its woolen sweater industry, Puyuan Town coordinated 120 million yuan in special funds at the city and town levels over 3 years to support market transformation, while using administrative power to lead comprehensive land consolidation, effectively promoting spatial function improvement and industrial upgrading.

S2 is the “human–capital” driven type. Configuration S2 has “people” and “finance” as core presence conditions, while “land,” “governance,” and “rights” are core absence conditions. This pathway covers 28.94% of the cases, with a consistency of 0.9051, indicating that even when land, governance, and rights-and-responsibilities mechanisms are all absent, the synergy between human resources and capital investment can still effectively improve spatial functions. A typical case of this pathway is Lingxi Town, Cangnan County. Guided by the orientation of “focusing on industry and talent,” Lingxi Town widely issued a “call for heroes” to attract more than 10 capable individuals, including the founder of “Cangping Kiln,” to return home for development. It simultaneously introduced over 50 million yuan in capital and revitalized more than 3,000 mu of idle land. Through the synergistic efforts of talent return and capital injection, it planned more than 20 projects, such as ceramic cultural and creative projects and pastoral coffee projects, effectively promoting spatial function improvement and rural industrial revitalization.

S3 is the multi-element synergy type. Configuration S3 has “people,” “land,” “finance,” and “rights” as core presence conditions, and “governance” as a core absence condition. This pathway covers 29.77% of the cases, with a consistency as high as 0.904, demonstrating the strong effect of multi-factor systemic synergy. A typical case of this pathway is Linghu Town, Nanxun District, Huzhou City. Nanxun District innovatively established a state-owned enterprise, the Strong Village and Prosperous People Group, to consolidate scattered fishponds across villages into contiguous areas. It invested more than 90 million yuan to build a digital modern fishery park and attracted young professionals specializing in aquaculture to contract fishponds and start businesses, effectively enhancing spatial functions and industrial resilience.

6.3.2 Configurational path analysis of non-high production–living–ecological space functions

Finance shortage emerges as a pervasive bottleneck leading to poor functionality, appearing in all non-high configurations and constituting a fundamental cause of functional failure. Furthermore, these configurations exhibit two typical types of predicament. The first is a “dual factor deficiency” type, in which a lack of financial resources coincides with the absence of other core development factors such as land or industry, resulting in severely inadequate systemic support. The second is the “rights–land failure” type, characterised by the presence of land and rights mechanisms against a backdrop of capital scarcity, yet these mechanisms fail to effectively integrate and steer the remaining resources, and may even exacerbate system-level inefficiencies due to misalignment. This suggests that non-high levels of PLES functions do not stem from the absence of a single condition, but rather from a “failure assemblage” formed between capital shortages and other factors or governance mechanisms.

6.4 Robustness test

This study conducted a robustness test of the “core-periphery” system configurations that generate high levels of PLES functions. Following established practices, the raw consistency threshold for cases was raised from 0.8 to 0.85 (White et al., 2021). A comparison of the results showed that the configurations of antecedent conditions remained identical. This robustness test confirms the robustness of the above findings.

7 Discussion and policy implications

7.1 Discussion

Using a township-level panel dataset for Zhejiang Province covering 2015–2022, this study comprehensively investigates the network mechanism and enhancement pathways of WRCLC on PLES by integrating the multi-period DID method, SNA, and fsQCA. Through theoretical development and empirical testing, the key findings are summarized below. First, the WRCLC pilot policy has a significant positive effect on PLES functions. Second, the policy improves the overall performance of PLES functions by increasing the degree centrality and closeness centrality of townships within the spatial correlation network of PLES. Third, the influence of the policy relies on the systematic interaction of the “core–periphery” system. The main enhancement pathways include the “capital–industry synergy” type, the “human–capital” driven type, and the “multi-element synergy” type. These pathways reveal, from different perspectives, the multiple condition combinations through which the policy objectives are achieved, thereby offering theoretical insights and practical guidance for differentially promoting WRCLC to enhance PLES functions.

7.2 Policy implications

First, the pilot work of comprehensive land consolidation should be continuously advanced and the policy implementation mechanism improved. It is recommended that, on the basis of summarizing pilot experience, a whole-process governance system of “planning–implementation–supervision” be established, and that the benefit distribution mechanism of land consolidation be improved to ensure that policy benefits are sustained. At the same time, at the legislative level of territorial spatial planning, rule-of-law safeguards and institutional coordination should be strengthened, the legislative process of the Territorial Spatial Planning Law should be accelerated, the legal relationship between comprehensive land consolidation and the territorial spatial planning system should be clarified, and comprehensive land consolidation should be incorporated into the implementation mechanism of territorial spatial planning. Where it is truly necessary to adjust planning during the implementation of consolidation, the corresponding trigger conditions, justification requirements, review bodies, and approval procedures should be further refined, and requirements for linking the adjusted planning results with the consolidation implementation plan should be stipulated. At the level of specialized legislation on land consolidation, the Land Consolidation Regulations may be revised to refine the technical standards for linking consolidation projects with spatial planning, and to stipulate that a spatial compliance review must be conducted before a consolidation project is approved, and that projects failing the review shall not be approved. The current Guidelines for the Implementation of Comprehensive Land Consolidation (Trial) already provide relatively specific policy guidance on implementation plans, project management, monitoring and supervision, and the protection of people’s rights and interests. On the basis of summarizing practical experience, the institutional arrangements of general applicability therein can be further transformed into stable administrative regulation rules, while specific technical standards and operational requirements can be left to departmental rules and local implementation norms. In response to the differences in local institutional conditions revealed by this study, the boundaries of responsibilities, coordination procedures, and accountability of departments such as natural resources, agriculture and rural affairs, ecological environment, and housing and urban-rural development at different stages of projects should be clarified, so as to reduce implementation deviations caused by departmental fragmentation and differences in local governance capacity.

Second, attention should be paid to spatial network development and regional synergistic efficiency should be enhanced. Policy implementation should focus on the structural position of townships within the regional network. By improving degree centrality and closeness centrality, a cross-regional platform for sharing resource factors should be established to promote the synergistic optimization of “production–living–ecological” (PLES) functions across a broader area. At the same time, long-term operation of the coordination mechanism should be guaranteed through legal means. Sections 13 (3) and Article 14 of Germany’s Federal Spatial Planning Act (Raumordnungsgesetz)17, through mechanisms such as joint regional planning, cross-regional planning cooperation, and regional networks, provide an institutionalized coordination pathway for coordinating spatial development that has close spatial linkages but extends beyond a single administrative region. This Act is not specialized legislation on comprehensive land consolidation, but the planning cooperation and coordination mechanisms it establishes for cross-administrative-region spaces have reference value for China in improving the regional coordination mechanism in comprehensive land consolidation. In light of China’s existing practices, the boundaries of rights and responsibilities across regions and departments should be further clarified in accordance with the law, and mechanisms for planning articulation, information sharing, interest coordination, and accountability should be improved, so that spatial network development and regional collaborative governance have a legal basis and operate stably, thereby enhancing overall regional synergistic efficiency.

Third, differentiated advancement strategies should be implemented. Each locality should choose suitable pathways according to its resource endowments to achieve an overall improvement in “production–living–ecological” (PLES) functions across the entire area. In this process, ecological priority and rule-of-law safeguards should be upheld. In territorial spatial planning, ecological function zoning techniques should be introduced. With the help of ecological sensitivity assessment, ecological carrying capacity analysis, and land ecological suitability evaluation, ecological protection zones, agricultural production zones, urban development zones, and ecological buffer zones should be scientifically delineated, and development intensity in different zones should be strictly controlled. The management and control of ecological protection red lines, permanent basic farmland, and urban development boundaries should be strengthened to ensure that land development conforms to the principle of ecological priority. At the same time, laws and regulations related to land resource protection should be improved. The “Avoid, Reduce, Compensate” (ERC) sequence established in France’s Environmental Code requires that environmental impacts be avoided with priority during planning and project implementation, that mitigation measures be taken for impacts that cannot be avoided, and that ecological compensation be implemented for residual impacts that still remain; for environmental impacts that cannot be adequately addressed through avoidance, mitigation, or compensation, the relevant projects shall not be permitted under the original plan18. This system places ecological protection requirements prior to development decisions and extends ecological impact control to the project implementation stage through compensation responsibilities, providing reference value for China in improving pre-development ecological assessment, environmental impact assessment, and ecological compensation mechanisms in comprehensive land consolidation. On this basis, China should further strengthen the environmental impact assessment system, strictly implement pre-development ecological assessment and environmental compensation mechanisms, increase penalties for illegal ecological destruction, and ensure that differentiated advancement pathways always operate within the track of the rule of law and the bottom line of ecology, thereby promoting the sustainable development and utilization of land resources.
